title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: On the right flank, commanded by Bagration, the battle had not yet begun at nine o'clock. Not wanting to agree to Dolgorukov's demand that he launch the attack, and hoping to avoid responsibility, Prince Bagration proposed sending a messenger to the commander in chief for instructions. Bagration knew perfectly well that since the distance between the two flanks was over six miles, even if the messenger wasn't killed along the way (which was very likely), and even if he managed to find the commander in chief (which would be extremely difficult), he still wouldn't make it back before evening.

Bagration let his large, expressionless, sleepy eyes wander across his staff, and the first face to catch his attention was the boyish face of Rostov, breathless with excitement and hope. He sent him.
"And if I meet His Majesty before I meet the commander in chief, your excellency?" Rostov asked, raising his hand to his cap.
"You may deliver the message to His Majesty," Dolgorukov cut in quickly, before Bagration could reply.

Having been relieved from picket duty, Rostov had managed to grab a few hours of sleep before dawn. He felt cheerful, bold, and full of purpose — his movements springy, his faith in his luck unshaken, and his overall state of mind one in which everything seems possible, pleasant, and easy.

Every one of his wishes was coming true that morning: a major battle was underway and he was part of it; better still, he was serving as orderly to the bravest general; and on top of that, he was riding off with a message for Kutuzov, and perhaps even for the sovereign himself. It was a bright morning, he had a strong horse under him, and his heart was full of joy and happiness. As soon as he received the order, he gave his horse its head and galloped along the line. At first he rode along Bagration's troops, which hadn't yet joined the fighting and stood motionless. Then he passed through the area held by Uvarov's cavalry, where he noticed preparations and a stir of activity. Beyond Uvarov's cavalry, he could clearly hear the sound of cannon and musket fire ahead of him. The firing grew louder.

In the fresh morning air, what he heard now was no longer the scattered musket shots at irregular intervals from before, followed by an occasional cannon blast. Instead, there was a continuous roll of musketry volleys from the slopes below Pratzen, broken by cannon reports so frequent that sometimes several of them merged together into a single roar.

He could see puffs of musketry smoke chasing each other down the hillsides, and clouds of cannon smoke rolling outward, spreading, and blending together. Through the smoke, he could also make out — by the glint of bayonets — moving masses of infantry and narrow lines of artillery with green ammunition wagons.

Rostov stopped his horse on a small hill to try to understand what was going on, but no matter how hard he strained his attention, he couldn't figure out or make sense of any of it. Down there in the smoke, men of some kind were moving around; lines of troops moved in the front and behind. But why, in which direction, and who they were — it was impossible to tell. Far from depressing or frightening him, the sights and sounds only heightened his energy and determination.
"Go on! Go on! Give it to them!" he cheered mentally at the sounds, and then continued galloping along the line, riding deeper and deeper into the area where the army was already engaged.
"What will happen there, I don't know, but it'll all work out!" Rostov thought.
After passing some Austrian troops, he noticed that the next section of the line — the Guards — was already in action.
"Even better! I'll get to see it up close," he thought.

He was riding almost along the front line. A cluster of men came galloping toward him — Uhlans, returning from an attack with their ranks in disarray. Rostov moved out of their way, involuntarily noticing that one of them was bleeding, and galloped on.

"That's not my concern," he thought. He hadn't gone many hundred yards when, off to his left, spanning the full width of the field, he saw an enormous body of cavalry in brilliant white uniforms mounted on black horses, trotting straight toward him and directly across his path. Rostov pushed his horse to full gallop to get clear of them, and he might have succeeded had they maintained their speed — but they kept going faster, and some of the horses were already at a full gallop. Rostov heard the pounding of hooves and the jingling of weapons, and he could see their horses, their figures, even their faces more and more clearly. These were the Horse Guards, advancing to attack the French cavalry that was riding to meet them.

The Horse Guards were galloping but still holding their horses in check. Rostov could already make out their faces and heard the command: "Charge!" shouted by an officer who was driving his thoroughbred to top speed. Fearing he would be crushed or dragged into the attack against the French, Rostov galloped along the front as fast as his horse could go, but still couldn't avoid them in time.

The last of the Horse Guards — a massive, pockmarked fellow — scowled angrily at seeing Rostov in his path, knowing a collision was inevitable. This Guardsman would certainly have knocked Rostov and his Bedouin horse flat (Rostov felt positively tiny and weak next to these enormous men and their horses), had Rostov not thought to crack his whip in front of the Guardsman's horse. The big black horse, sixteen hands high, shied and pinned back its ears. But the pockmarked Guardsman dug in his huge spurs, and the horse flicked its tail, stretched out its neck, and charged forward even faster. The Horse Guards had barely passed Rostov when he heard them shout "Hurrah!" and, looking back, he saw their front ranks tangled up with foreign cavalry wearing red shoulder pieces — probably French. He could see nothing more after that, because suddenly cannon began firing from somewhere and smoke covered everything.

At that moment, as the Horse Guards disappeared into the smoke beyond him, Rostov hesitated: should he gallop after them, or continue on to where he'd been sent? This was the brilliant charge of the Horse Guards that stunned even the French. Rostov was horrified to learn later that out of that entire mass of huge, handsome men — all those brilliant, wealthy young officers and cadets who had galloped past him on their thousand-ruble horses — only eighteen survived the charge.
"Why should I envy them? My chance hasn't passed, and maybe I'll see the Emperor any minute now!" Rostov thought, and galloped on.

When he came level with the Foot Guards, he became aware that cannonballs were flying nearby — not so much from hearing them as from seeing the anxious looks on the soldiers' faces and the forced, unnatural solemnity of the officers.
As he passed behind one of the Foot Guard regiment's lines, a voice called out his name.
"Rostov!"
"What?" he answered, not recognizing Boris.
"Guess what — we were in the front line! Our regiment attacked!" Boris said with the bright, happy smile of a young man who has been under fire for the first time.
Rostov stopped.
"Really? How did it go?"

"We drove them back!" Boris said excitedly, becoming talkative. "Can you imagine it?" And he launched into a story about how the Guards had taken up their position and spotted troops ahead, assumed they were Austrians, and then suddenly realized from the cannonballs raining down on them that they were actually on the front line and had to go into action unexpectedly. Rostov spurred his horse before Boris had finished.
"Where are you headed?" Boris asked.
"To deliver a message to His Majesty."

"There he is!" Boris said, thinking Rostov had said "His Highness," and pointing to the Grand Duke, who stood a hundred paces away in his helmet and Horse Guards jacket, his high shoulders squared and brows knitted, shouting something at a pale, white-uniformed Austrian officer.
"But that's the Grand Duke — I need the commander in chief, or the Emperor," Rostov said, about to spur his horse forward.

"Count! Count!" Berg shouted, running up from the other side, just as eager as Boris. "Count! I've been wounded in my right hand" — and he showed his bleeding hand wrapped in a handkerchief — "and I stayed at the front! I held my sword in my left hand, Count. Our whole family — the von Bergs — have always been knights!"
He said something more, but Rostov didn't wait to hear it and rode away.

Having passed the Guards and crossed an open stretch, Rostov — wanting to avoid being caught in front of the first line again, as he had been during the Horse Guards' charge — followed the line of reserves, giving a wide berth to the areas with the heaviest musket and cannon fire. Suddenly he heard musket fire very close, directly in front of him and behind the Russian positions — somewhere the enemy should not have been.

"What's going on?" he thought. "The enemy behind our army? That's impossible!" And suddenly he was seized by a wave of fear — fear for himself and for the outcome of the whole battle. "But whatever happens," he told himself, "there's no way around it now. I have to find the commander in chief right here, and if everything is lost, then I'll die with the rest."
The sense of dread that had suddenly gripped Rostov only grew stronger the farther he rode into the area behind the village of Pratzen, which was teeming with troops of every kind.
"What does it mean? What's happening? Who are they firing at? Who's doing the firing?" Rostov kept asking as he encountered Russian and Austrian soldiers running in confused crowds across his path.
"The devil only knows! Everyone's been killed! It's all over!" he was told in Russian, German, and Czech by the fleeing crowds, who understood what was happening no better than he did.
"Kill the Germans!" one man shouted.
"To hell with them — the traitors!"
"Damn these Russians!" a German muttered.
Footnote: "Hang these Russians!"

Several wounded men came along the road, and curses, screams, and groans all merged into a general uproar. Then the firing died away. Rostov later learned that Russian and Austrian soldiers had been shooting at each other.

"My God! What does this all mean?" he thought. "And right here, where the Emperor himself might see it any moment. But no — these must just be a handful of rotten soldiers. It'll be over soon. It can't really be as bad as it looks — it just can't! If I can just get past them — quickly, quickly!"

The very idea of defeat and flight could not enter Rostov's mind. Even though he saw French cannon and French troops on the Pratzen Heights — the very place where he'd been sent to look for the commander in chief — he could not, and would not, believe it.
